background.definition: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a highly prevalent herpes virus, which causes disease in transplant recipients and persons with AIDS. It also causes a congenital infection in newborns. It generally causes mild illness or a mononucleosis-like syndrome in healthy children and adults.

list.listitem: The annual incidence of CMV is 1.6% among susceptible persons between the ages of 12 and 49 years.
Incidence during pregnancy among seronegative women between the ages of 20 and 49 years is 1.4% among non-Hispanic whites; 3.4% among non-Hispanic blacks; and 3.8% among Mexican Americans.
One in 150 children is born with congenital CMV infection, and 1 in 750 children is born with or develops permanent disabilities caused by CMV.
In the United States, 36% of children between the ages of 6 and 11 years are seropositive for CMV.
A total of 91% of Americans are seropositive by 40 years of age.
CMV is a herpes virus, closely related to the human herpes viruses 6 and 7.

CMV initially infects epithelial cells of the salivary glands and replicates slowly, taking days to weeks to show cytopathic changes. This infection causes cell enlargement with intranuclear inclusions and may infect all organs.
In congenital infections, CMV causes growth retardation in utero, hearing loss, ocular abnormalities, intracranial calcifications and microcephaly, hepatosplenomegaly, petechiae, and jaundice.
Following organ transplantation, CMV causes pneumonitis, hepatitis, GI disease, meningoencephalitis, and myocarditis.
In patients with AIDS (CD4 <50), CMV causes retinitis and inflammation of the GI tract, most commonly the esophagus and colon.

Pregnant women and HIV-infected individuals should avoid secretions and wash hands carefully around infants and young children, since they often excrete CMV in urine and saliva. This is supported by a systematic review of 7 non-randomized studies.C
CMV is shed in semen, saliva, and cervicovaginal secretions. Transmission can be prevented by use of latex condoms. C
Obtain baseline CMV antibody titers for all HIV patients at low risk for previous exposure. C

Prophylaxis with anti-CMV medications reduces CMV disease and CMV-associated mortality in solid organ transplant recipients who are seropositive for CMV and in those who have received CMV-positive organ transplants. Pre-emptive antiviral treatment of CMV infection in this group of patients appears to be no more effective than antiviral prophylaxis. IgG is not indicated for prophylaxis in this group of patients.B

Prophylaxis of patients with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant with letermovir reduces CMV infection. Prophylaxis of patients with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant with valganciclovir does not prevent complications of late CMV infection.A
Prophylaxis of pregnant women with hyperimmune globulin does not prevent congenital CMV.B
Order a strep test, monospot, and CBC in febrile patients with pharyngitis, adenopathy, and fatigue. C
In patients with persistent mononucleosis symptoms, order CMV IgM, herpes and respiratory virus polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and consider acute HIV infection. C
Obtain TORCH titers and viral cultures or PCR of urine or saliva in newborns presenting with symptoms consistent with congenital CMV. C

list.listitem: In AIDS patients and organ transplant recipients, viremia and/or positive viral cultures of biopsy specimens do not establish a diagnosis of CMV disease, since patients may have CMV present without disease.
Mucosal ulcerations on endoscopy combined with a biopsy showing characteristic intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusions are required for the diagnosis of CMV colitis.

The diagnosis of CMV esophagitis requires large, shallow ulcers of the distal esophagus and biopsy evidence of intranuclear inclusion bodies in the endothelial cells with an inflammatory reaction at the edge of the ulcer.
In immunocompetent hosts, CMV may be asymptomatic or cause a mononucleosis-like syndrome, with prolonged fever, lymphadenopathy, and pharyngitis.

In AIDS patients, retinitis is the most common clinical manifestation of CMV end-organ disease and presents with floaters, scotomata, or peripheral visual field defects. The ophthalmoscopic appearance of CMV retinitis includes perivascular fluffy yellow-white retinal infiltrates, with or without intraretinal hemorrhage.
CMV colitis presents with fever, weight loss, anorexia, abdominal pain, debilitating diarrhea, and malaise.
CMV esophagitis presents with fever, odynophagia, nausea, and occasionally mid-epigastric or retrosternal pain.
CMV neurologic disease causes dementia, ventriculoencephalitis, or ascending polyradiculomyelopathy.

Order a strep test, monospot, and CBC in febrile patients with pharyngitis, adenopathy, and fatigue. In patients with persistent mononucleosis symptoms, especially if they have elevated transaminases and atypical lymphocytosis, order CMV IgM, herpes and respiratory virus PCR, and consider acute HIV infection. Acute HIV infection confirmation requires an HIV PCR, not an antibody test.

The IgM antibody is present 2 weeks after the initial infection and persists for several months. A 4-fold increase in IgG in specimens obtained at least 2 weeks apart is the gold standard serologic test.
CMV viral culture can be positive within 2 days, but is not definitively negative for 3 weeks.

In a study of 52 immunocompetent hosts (40 of whom were pregnant), a CMV PCR of blood leukocytes was 57% sensitive and 100% specific at 1 month. Virus levels were low by all assays and did not correlate with clinical course of infection, intrauterine transmission, or severity of outcome.

A screening study of 34,989 infants found that CMV PCR of both liquid-saliva and dried-saliva had high sensitivity and specificity. Liquid-saliva CMV PCR sensitivity was 100% (95% CI, 95.8-100) and specificity was 99.9% (95% CI, 99.9-100). Dried-saliva CMV PCR sensitivity was 97.4% (95% CI, 90.8-99.7) and specificity was 99.9% (95% CI, 99.9-100).
See Figure 1 in Infectious Mononucleosis chapter for a suggested approach to initial evaluation.
In patients with persistent mononucleosis symptoms, order CMV IgM, herpes and respiratory virus PCR, and consider acute HIV infection.
CMV is self-limited in immunocompetent hosts and antiviral treatment has not been studied. C
Treatment of immunosuppressed individuals with specific antivirals (ganciclovir, foscarnet, cidofovir) needs to be individualized and guided by specialist advice. B
Valacyclovir can reduce the likelihood of vertical transmission during pregnancy (NNT = 7).A
Drug therapy has not been studied in immunocompetent hosts.
Therapy for immunosuppression-related CMV retinitis is based on the location and severity of the lesion(s), underlying immune suppression, other medications, and the ability to adhere to treatment.
Colitis or esophagitis is treated with IV ganciclovir or foscarnet.
Antiretroviral therapy should be started promptly for those with acute CMV retinitis and/or GI disease.

Treatment of neonates with symptomatic congenital CMV with valganciclovir for 6 months (compared to 6 weeks) was not associated with short-term hearing improvement, but was associated with modest long-term hearing improvement and neurodevelopmental outcomes.

In an RCT, 123 women with primary CMV infection (gestational age 5-26 weeks) were randomized to hyperimmune globulin or placebo. There was no benefit, and women in the treatment group had more adverse obstetrical events.

A meta-analysis of 3 RCTs involving 527 pregnant mothers who had acquired CMV either periconceptionally or during pregnancy showed that valacyclovir until amniocentesis at 21 to 22 weeks gestational age significantly reduced the rate of vertical transmission, as evidenced by lower CMV positivity on amniocentesis (11% vs 26 % , p < 0.001, NNT =7), with a 2.1% adverse event rate (primarily acute obstructive renal failure due to crystallization of the valacyclovir by-product in the renal tubules).
In AIDS patients with CMV opportunistic infection, chronic maintenance therapy should be continued for life, unless immune reconstitution occurs as a result of antiretroviral therapy.
One in 750 children is born with or develops permanent disabilities because of CMV. C
CMV acquired at the time of birth or from breast milk is typically asymptomatic and is not associated with significant sequelae. C
Immunocompetent individuals with symptomatic CMV usually recover fully in days to weeks. C
The Centers for Disease Control does not recommend screening of pregnant women.

In an RCT, 123 women with primary CMV infection (gestational age 5-26 weeks) were randomized to hyperimmune globulin or placebo. There was no benefit, and women in the treatment group had more adverse obstetrical events.

A meta-analysis of 3 RCTs involving 527 pregnant mothers who had acquired CMV either periconceptionally or during pregnancy showed that valacyclovir until amniocentesis at 21 to 22 weeks gestational age significantly reduced the rate of vertical transmission, as evidenced by lower CMV positivity on amniocentesis (11% vs 26 % , p < 0.001, NNT =6.9), with a 2.1% adverse event rate (primarily acute obstructive renal failure due to crystallization of the valacyclovir by-product in the renal tubules).

Although some studies have suggested that maternal CMV infection during pregnancy may be associated with increased risk of childhood cancer, results are inconsistent and not significant when restricted to high-quality studies (effect size 1.73 vs 1.00, 95% CI 0.68-4.39).

Most infants with a congenital CMV infection are asymptomatic at birth but may present with jaundice, petechiae, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, growth restriction, and hydrops. CMV is the leading cause of congenital hearing loss (12.6% of children with congenital CMV have profound/severe hearing loss).

CMV acquired after birth is self-limited and not associated with long-term sequelae in immunocompetent hosts. A systematic review of 26 studies found low rates of maternal-child CMV transmission via breast milk to premature infants and no evidence of long-term sequelae.
